## 🎯 Goal

This vignette walks through the process of fitting Septoria tritici blotch severity data in Indiana using FraNchEstYN.
We will use the example datasets bundled with the package:

- **`weather_indiana`**: daily weather data (NASA POWER)
- **`reference_indiana`**: digitized disease observations from [Shaner & Buechley (1995)](https://www.apsnet.org/publications/plantdisease/backissues/Documents/1995Articles/PlantDisease79n09_928.PDF)
- **`management_indiana`**: sowing and crop management metadata from the same article.

```{r, include=F}
#| label: setup

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)
```

## 📦 Packages

We load the FraNchEstYN package plus some helper libraries for data handling, tables, and plotting.

```{r}
#| label: franchLoad

library(FraNchEstYN)
library(tidyverse)
library(kableExtra)
library(plotly)
```

## 📥 Data loading

The three Indiana datasets are included with the package.
Below we load them and preview a few rows to illustrate their structure.

```{r}
#| label: data_loading

data(weather_indiana)
data(reference_indiana)
data(management_indiana)
```

```{r}
#| label: data_showing
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Minimal preview: first 6 rows of the most relevant columns
kable(
  weather_indiana %>%
    select(site, year, month, day, tx, tn, p, rad) %>%
    slice_head(n = 3),
  caption = "weather_indiana — daily weather (first rows)"
)

kable(
  reference_indiana %>%
    select(site, year, DOY, FINT, Disease) %>%
    slice_head(n = 3),
  caption = "reference_indiana — disease observations"
)

kable(
  management_indiana %>%
    select(site, crop, variety, year, sowingDOY) %>%
    slice_head(n = 3),
  caption = "management_indiana — management metadata (first 6 rows)"
)
```

## ⚙️ Parameters

In FraNchEstYN, **crop** and **disease** processes are controlled by parameter sets describing physiological and epidemiological traits.

In this vignette we are only interested in **canopy light interception and disease severity**, not yield formation.

- For wheat: start from defaults, disable calibration of traits unrelated to light interception, and keep canopy dynamics active.

- For Septoria: start from defaults, and disable calibration of yield-loss damage mechanisms.

```{r}
#| label: parameters

# Load default parameters for wheat
thisCropParam <- cropParameters$wheat

# Disable all calibration, then selectively re-enable light interception
thisCropParam <- set_calibration_flags(
  thisCropParam,
  disable = c(
    "PartitioningMaximum",
    "TbaseCrop",
    "TmaxCrop",
    "ToptCrop",
    "FloweringStart",
    "RadiationUseEfficiency",
    "CycleLength",
    "HalfIntSenescence"
  )
)

# Load default parameters for Septoria
thisDiseaseParam <- diseaseParameters$septoria

# Disable calibration for yield-loss damage mechanisms
thisDiseaseParam <- set_calibration_flags(
  thisDiseaseParam,
  disable = c(
    "RUEreducerDamage",
    "LightStealerDamage",
    "SenescenceAcceleratorDamage",
    "AssimilateSappersDamage",
    "Topt",
    "Tmax",
    "RelativeHumidityCritical",
    "RelativeHumidityNotLimiting"
  )
)
thisDiseaseParam$OuterInoculumShapeRelease$value <- 2
```

## 🔧 Calibration model call

With data and parameters prepared, we can call the **FraNchEstYN calibration engine**.
Here we fit both crop and disease model parameters simultaneously, using the Indiana datasets.

Key settings:

- **start_end**: simulation period (1971–1991, as in the article)
- **api_key**: required for external API calls, but *not used here*
- **franchy_message**: set to `FALSE` to silence fun messages 😉
- **iterations**: number of optimization iterations (`999`, as in the article)
- **calibration**: scope of calibration (`"all"` means crop + disease)

This returns a model object df containing diagnostics, parameters, and simulation outputs.

```{r, eval=T}
#| label: calibration
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: "hide"

start_end <- c(1971, 1991)
api_key <- "xxx" # not used here for LLM
franchy_message <- FALSE
iterations <- 999 # as in the article; the more iterations, the safer the results
calibration <- "all" # calibrate both crop and disease

df <- franchestyn(
  weather_data = weather_indiana,
  management_data = management_indiana,
  reference_data = reference_indiana,
  cropParameters = thisCropParam,
  diseaseParameters = thisDiseaseParam,
  start_end = start_end,
  calibration = calibration,
  apikey = api_key,
  franchy_message = franchy_message,
  iterations = iterations
)
```

## 📊 Outputs & results

### ⚖️ Parameter plots

Plots show parameter ranges, defaults, and calibrated values:

- **Black / grey lines** = allowable parameter ranges
- 🔵 **Blue vertical line** = default value
- 🔴 **Red dot** = calibrated value (if calibration was enabled)

Note: only the crop parameters controlling canopy light interception are calibrated; all other crop parameters remain at their defaults (blue line only).

```{r, eval=T, fig.alt=c("Parameter ranges, default values and calibrated values for the wheat crop parameters in Indiana", "Parameter ranges, default values and calibrated values for the Septoria disease parameters in Indiana")}
#| label: diagnostics
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

df$diagnostics$calibration$plots$crop
df$diagnostics$calibration$plots$disease
```

### 📏 Calibration metrics (Disease Severity)

We summarise calibration accuracy for disease severity across seasons using Bias, MAE, RMSE, correlation, R², and NSE.

```{r, eval=T}
#| label: metrics
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

metrics_ds <- df$diagnostics$metrics %>%
  filter(Variable == "DisSev") %>%
  select(GrowingSeason, n, Bias, MAE, RMSE, r, R2, NSE) %>%
  arrange(GrowingSeason) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

# Overall row: all observations pooled across seasons
sim_obs <- df$outputs$simulation %>%
  filter(!is.na(as.numeric(DiseaseSeverityRef))) %>%
  transmute(obs = as.numeric(DiseaseSeverityRef), sim = DiseaseSeverity)

overall <- with(
  sim_obs,
  tibble(
    GrowingSeason = "Overall",
    n = length(obs),
    Bias = mean(sim - obs),
    MAE = mean(abs(sim - obs)),
    RMSE = sqrt(mean((sim - obs)^2)),
    r = cor(obs, sim),
    R2 = cor(obs, sim)^2,
    NSE = 1 - sum((obs - sim)^2) / sum((obs - mean(obs))^2)
  )
) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

metrics_ds <- bind_rows(
  metrics_ds %>% mutate(GrowingSeason = as.character(GrowingSeason)),
  overall
)

kable(
  metrics_ds,
  caption = "Calibration metrics for disease severity (DisSev)",
  align = "lrrrrrrr"
) %>%
  kable_styling(
    full_width = FALSE,
    font_size = 11,
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed")
  ) %>%
  row_spec(nrow(metrics_ds), bold = TRUE) # highlight Overall row
```

## 📈 Simulation outputs

### 🗂️ Season summary

A compact table of disease severity outcomes for each growing season: final severity, peak, timing, and area-under-curve.
In all model outputs, `GrowingSeason` is the **sowing** year: season 1972 is the crop sown in autumn 1972 and harvested in 1973 (the year used in `reference_indiana` and in the article).

```{r}
#| label: summary-table
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

summary <- df$outputs$summary

summary %>%
  arrange(GrowingSeason) %>%
  select(-c(Variety, YieldAttainable:AGBActual)) |>
  mutate(dplyr::across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  kable(caption = "summary of simulated disease severity") %>%
  kable_styling(
    full_width = FALSE,
    font_size = 11,
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed")
  )
```

### 🗺️️ Multi-season overview (static)

Facetted plots across seasons showing dynamics of inoculum, latent and sporulating tissue, canopy light interception, and disease severity vs. observations.

```{r}
#| label: chart1
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-alt: "Simulated and observed Septoria tritici blotch severity, inoculum, latent and sporulating tissue and canopy light interception for each growing season in Indiana, 1971 to 1991"

outputs <- df$outputs$simulation

ggplot(outputs, aes(x = as.Date(Date, format = "%m/%d/%Y"))) +
  geom_area(aes(y = HTtimeRinoculum, fill = "HTtimeRinoculum"), alpha = .3) +
  geom_area(aes(y = Latent, fill = "Latent"), alpha = .7) +
  geom_area(aes(y = Sporulating, fill = "Sporulating"), alpha = .7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Susceptible, color = "Susceptible"), size = .5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Affected, color = "Affected"), size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Dead, color = "Dead"), alpha = .5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = LightInterception, color = "LightInterception"), size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = LightIntHealthy, color = "LightIntHealthy"), size = 1) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = LightInterceptionRef, color = "LightInterceptionRef"),
    size = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(y = DiseaseSeverity, color = "DiseaseSeverity"), size = 1) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = as.numeric(DiseaseSeverityRef), color = "DiseaseSeverityRef"),
    shape = 21,
    size = 2.2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~GrowingSeason, ncol = 6, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    x = "Date",
    y = "State variable / Severity",
    color = "Legend",
    fill = "Legend"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "HTtimeRinoculum" = "yellow4",
      "Latent" = "gold",
      "Sporulating" = "orange"
    )
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Susceptible" = "green4",
      "Affected" = "red",
      "Dead" = "red4",
      "LightInterception" = "black",
      "LightIntHealthy" = "green4",
      "LightInterceptionRef" = "black",
      "DiseaseSeverity" = "blue",
      "DiseaseSeverityRef" = "blue"
    )
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.box = "vertical",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8)
  )
```

### 🎯 1972–73 deep-dive (interactive)

An interactive plot of the 1972–73 season (sown in autumn 1972, observed and harvested in 1973) lets us hover over state variables and observed values.

```{r}
#| label: chart2
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-alt: "Interactive plot of simulated and observed Septoria severity and canopy light interception in Indiana for the 1972 season"

season_outputs <- outputs %>% dplyr::filter(GrowingSeason == 1972)

p <- ggplot(season_outputs, aes(x = as.Date(Date, format = "%m/%d/%Y"))) +
  geom_area(aes(y = HTtimeRinoculum, fill = "HTtimeRinoculum"), alpha = .3) +
  geom_area(aes(y = Latent, fill = "Latent"), alpha = .7) +
  geom_area(aes(y = Sporulating, fill = "Sporulating"), alpha = .7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Susceptible, color = "Susceptible"), size = .5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Affected, color = "Affected"), size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Dead, color = "Dead"), alpha = .5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = LightInterception, color = "LightInterception"), size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = LightIntHealthy, color = "LightIntHealthy"), size = 1) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = LightInterceptionRef, color = "LightInterceptionRef"),
    size = 1
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(y = DiseaseSeverity, color = "DiseaseSeverity"), size = 1) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = as.numeric(DiseaseSeverityRef), color = "DiseaseSeverityRef"),
    shape = 21,
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Date",
    y = "State variable / Severity",
    title = "1972–73 season (GrowingSeason = 1972)",
    color = "Legend",
    fill = "Legend"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "HTtimeRinoculum" = "yellow4",
      "Latent" = "gold",
      "Sporulating" = "orange"
    )
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Susceptible" = "green4",
      "Affected" = "red",
      "Dead" = "red4",
      "LightInterception" = "black",
      "LightIntHealthy" = "green4",
      "LightInterceptionRef" = "black",
      "DiseaseSeverity" = "blue",
      "DiseaseSeverityRef" = "blue"
    )
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",

# Convert to plotly and fix legend placement
plotly::ggplotly(p) %>%
  plotly::layout(
    legend = list(

      x = 0, # align left
      y = -0.3 # move below plot
    )

## 🔄 Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV)

This vignette runs the full-dataset calibration only.
The article also reports a leave-one-season-out cross-validation over the 19 growing seasons with observations (sown 1972–1990, harvested 1973–1991): each season is withheld in turn, the model is calibrated on the remaining 18 seasons (333 iterations per fold) and the withheld season is then predicted with calibration switched off.

Note that in `reference_indiana` the column `year` is the **harvest** year, whereas simulation outputs are labelled by `GrowingSeason` (the **sowing** year).
When withholding a season, remove the reference rows with `year == GrowingSeason + 1`.

The four disease parameters fixed above (`Topt`, `Tmax`, `RelativeHumidityCritical`, `RelativeHumidityNotLimiting`), together with crop `CycleLength` and `HalfIntSenescence`, were identified in a preliminary LOOCV run as having negligible variability across folds (CV < 5%).

LOOCV results (Willmott's d, Pearson r, RMSE, MBE) are shown in Figure 5 and discussed in Section 3.3.2 of the article.
The LOOCV takes about 45 minutes and is not run here; the full script is available in the package repository (`tests/submission/revision/file analysis/indiana/indiana.R`).

## 📝 Key take-home messages

- FraNchEstYN successfully calibrated disease severity for Septoria tritici in Indiana across two decades of observations.

- Crop parameters were mostly fixed (default values) — only canopy light interception was active, while disease parameters were calibrated.

- The framework provides diagnostics, metrics, parameter estimates, and simulations in a consistent structure, ready for analysis or visualization.

## 🚀 Next steps

This vignette showed how to calibrate Septoria tritici blotch severity in Indiana using bundled datasets.
From here, you might want to:

🌎 Explore other environments: replace weather_indiana, reference_indiana, and management_indiana with datasets from different sites or years.

🌾 Switch crops or pathogens: try other parameter sets available in cropParameters and diseaseParameters.

🎛️ Experiment with calibration scope:

- `"all"` → calibrate both crop and disease models
- `"crop"` or `"disease"` → focus on one component only

📊 Analyze uncertainty: increase the number of iterations or run multiple calibration replicates to assess stability of parameter estimates.

🛠️ Extend the pipeline: integrate with your own management practices or link outputs to yield-loss models.
